text: I'm going to go ahead and call this meeting of the Board's Information Technology Committee meeting to order. Got a pretty stacked agenda today, so we're going to take as much time as we need, but move through it quickly and efficiently at the same time.

First up, we have a presentation on the FCPS Board of Supervisors IT Committee, Joint IT Committee update, and that will be followed by some discussion. Chairman, do you want to make any introductory remarks on this one?

Just very brief, I want to thank the staff who's been working on this and importantly also the members of the Board of Supervisors and School Board who have been working on this in a collaborative manner because this is so important. It is very important for both from a budgeting standpoint but just from an efficiency standpoint.

And I know it's taken a lot of staff time and effort. And these committees, they always look great on paper. Sometimes they produce good products. Sometimes they just take up a lot of time. And in this case, it looks good on paper and has produced some good results.

And so I just want to thank the folks who have been working on that and just remind my colleagues that, you know, these are great opportunities for members of our two boards to get together with staff and vet a lot of the issues that then our entire boards don't need to vet and bring forward good recommendations for efficiencies and improvements that we can make, in this case, both across the county and the public school system.

So really just a word of thanks and encouragement and appreciation for the staff time that it's taken. County Executive Hill, you had a wave in your hand there. Yeah, thank you, Supervisor Chairman Harrity, and thank you for those words, Chairman McKay. And I want to thank Supervisors Stork and Alcorn.

After this meeting is complete, we're going to also put together a net for expectations. So we all have it documented about what our next processes, our next steps will be. I want to thank Gotham and his team, as well as Alicia, Siri, McCormick, and all the folks that were involved.

It is about collaboration. It's about making sure that our residents receive the services we provide at a high level. And I think we can do a lot of good work together if we can collaborate on a lot of the things that we're looking into. So I just want to say thank you.

But the NIP will be forthcoming. Okay, Maura, I'm turning it over to you or is it Alicia? I get the honor this morning. Good morning. Welcome to the Information Technology Committee meeting. I am standing in for Matt Harrison today.

Unfortunately, he had to have a medical procedure. He's doing well. He's recovering at home and he hated to miss the fun today. He may actually be watching, so that's the good news. So we're going to go through today the agenda that Supervisor Herity spoke to, which is the review of the Joint Board and Fairfax County School Board IT Committee meeting and the discussions and updates and recommendations that are coming out of that.

We also will go over the affidavit board matter and where we are right now in terms of a status update, and we will go over the summary of the ITPAC letter to the board as well as a presentation by their chair. So joining me today to go through all of those agenda items are Maura Power, our Deputy Director slash Chief Technology Officer with the Department of Information Technology, Gautam Sethi, who is here from the Fairfax County Schools as their Chief Information Technology Officer.

Anita Rao, our Deputy Director and Chief Applications Officer within the Department of Information Technology. And Sean Rastetter, our Chair of ITPAC, who will be doing the presentation for their letter and his thoughts on our budget and other things that we're trending on and the discussions there, as well as Guy Swo from ITPAC.

So we're very excited to have everyone provide their input today and answer any questions that you might have. And as the county executive said, this discussion in particular as it relates to the Joint Information Technology Committee will inform that final report that we're going to send out. So we're really happy to hear any discussion or concerns or other things that you have for us.

Thank you, Alicia. Thank you, everyone. And again, I also want to say thank you to the Board of Supervisors and the school board members who helped us participate on this joint committee. It really was a good effort in where we were able to actually work together. I think in the years that I've been here in the county, I haven't seen this amount of collaboration between our IT group and the school.

So I think that was a benefit just from the get-go. So moving into what we did, obviously this presentation is focused a little bit around process, and then we'll get into kind of the findings and the outcomes that we have. So the joint committee, just to level set, was set up so that we could find operational efficiencies, so that we could find opportunities for ourselves to find some cost savings or some cost avoidances and to really look at our resources and how we can kind of optimize some of the resources that we have there.

As we established this committee, we did start with a charter. So we used that charter to set our guiding principles, and we really wanted to make sure that we were using strategic thinking around our use of technology and our technology assets and services.

We definitely wanted to be good stewards of the Fairfax County dollars and given the ongoing budget uncertainties, as we all know. We also, we are accustomed to having high quality IT services, and we didn't want to look at reducing any of those services.

We wanted to make sure that we had a commitment to continuing with high quality services and high quality IT, as well as making sure that from a security and maintenance and from an innovation perspective that we're still underscoring those as principles.

because, again, you know, we have to be very, very secure with all of our applications and all of the data that we work with, both in the schools and in the county. So moving on, you know, we had the work group, we actually, or we had the committee, we had to finalize and have a work group, right?

So getting into the details, once the committee met, we took our additional teams of SMEs and we worked through really trying to dig into some details. So we reviewed our individual technology investments. We looked at renewal cycles for software, for hardware, and we did some in-depth discovery sessions with key vendors.

I also want to underscore that a lot of the work that we did once we convened down into a work group was really -- it was supported by that SAP endeavor. So having a joint procurement system, which was something that this board has encouraged in the past between us and the schools really allowed us to do some deep analysis and deep understanding of where we're purchasing and what we're purchasing from an IT perspective.

And I think from the leadership teams and both at the school side as well as on the county side, we also underscored with all of our teams, you know, you guys are in the day-to-day, you're working through work with your counterparts at the schools, learn from each other, talk with each other. And I think as we started to align that approach and siphon it down to all staff, we really started to see the teams dig in on being in this aligned approach.

So continuing with our work group, we had a small sprint cycle in which we worked in. We started in October of 25, really starting going through meeting weekly, if not more. We engaged with some of our vendors as well, doing books of business reviews.

Again, as I mentioned, we spent a lot of time working on the data analysis to align and to look at those products and services, the places where we did have overlap. And then we worked again with our different teams, having our SMEs talk with each other. As we worked through that, we then started to craft our strategy for how we were going to approach the cost optimization, which now I'm going to hand over to Gautam to go into more detail.

Good morning. You can get to the next slide. As technologies often do, we took the very large task and broke it down into its subunits. What emerged was two distinct pathways, which we'll discuss a little bit.

The tactical pathway, which was a quick sprint in the next two months, three months, to be able to come back with some cost optimizations. And then the strategic pathway, which led us into a longer journey to say, where do we go from here? What are the opportunities where we can intentionally collaborate and build future value for the county and the school division as a whole?

Next slide. In our tactical pathway, we worked, as Mara was mentioning, overlaying large vendor purchases among the two entities. The goal was to force to be able to look at, say, if you're buying similar items, is there value in per unit pricing for those items? This could be hardware units. It could be software units. The also sought alignment on long-term objectives, where we were looking at how should we be architecting solutions in the future where, when permitted through regulations or through privacy requirements, we could share some entities and units of collaboration. An

example that emerged was data centers. We have data centers within the county. It's run in an old elementary school building, which has been something that has supported us for a while, but we would love to have a modern enterprise data center approach, which can be a collaboration that we can work towards. You will also hear about some of these opportunities in the future slides.

Two key among the structural was a user base that we serve as individual entities. Fairfax County public school serves about 250,000-ish, which includes 180,000 students, staff, and then a larger population, which is our parent community, which is also overlapping potentially with the Fairfax County government's community of service. And amongst 200 buildings which are spread over the county, FCG supports regulated environments. The key data privacy regulation and compliance needs require technology provisioning and support creates variance in our staffing loads and cost

basis. Additionally, some of the vendors also emerged as saying that we have very distinct pricing strategies. What they may give to the school district as a school entity or an education entity may not be what they will offer as price points and strategies to a county government.

Separate and distinct, and they came back with those as responses to our optimization questions. While the majority of technology investments at Fairfax County focus on ed tech, This is devices for students.

As you know, every student, since the pandemic, has had a device issued to them when they need to use it. We also focus heavily on educational tools, so instructional tools in the classroom, which are used by teachers, or also student information collection databases, which will be very distinct and unique in Fairfax public school technology operations, as opposed to FCGs.

We did engage with the largest providers of our business and office technology to both of us, Exploring opportunities for price consolidation and discounting. As I had mentioned earlier, the vendor, specifically that vendor, which was a larger sort of purchase across both our books, budget books, told us that they do not overlay and overlap the pricing points between us as a school district and the county government.

Therefore, they would want to maintain them as separate books of contracts for both those entities. Thank you. Thank you. So I know he spoke to some of the things where we don't align. I'm going to talk about some of the opportunities where we actually did find some alignment because I think that's where we find these efficiencies and these costs, avoidances and savings.

So one of the major opportunities we saw was in that network infrastructure area. So when I'm talking about network infrastructure, I'm talking about routing, I'm talking about switches. And from there, we found that there were, we used the same platforms, right?

So we're using the same tools, we're using the same hardware. However, we were actually approaching it across several different reseller contracts. So for those of you who aren't aware, IT operates a lot like car dealerships, right?

So like the manufacturers, they're the ones that are making the cars, and you have to go to a dealership to buy it. The same thing happens with IT. We have folks who are creating hardware, who are creating software, and we have to go through resellers to actually purchase that software.

So when we look at our network infrastructure, when we're looking at the hardware related to switches and routers, there were often opportunities with different price points, right? So maybe there was a different discountage percentage point that we were receiving, that the schools were receiving.

So as we started with this committee, as we started with the intentional conversations, we were starting to notice those differences. And again, as we looked at the data from our SAP system, we found that for the same exact equipment, we were purchasing off of three different reseller contracts.

So we had an opportunity to kind of align, to strategically come together. Now, the discounts aren't huge, right? So it's small dollars that we're working with, but it was still an opportunity. And as we go through this, every little bit helps is how I see it. You know, that's how we manage things at home as well.

So every place where you can get that additional 2%, 3%, or whatever you can find, those were some opportunities that we found. Also around wireless access points, right? We're trying to put Wi-Fi, make Wi-Fi available for everyone in the schools as well as every, you know, the employees here in Fairfax County as well as the public.

We're buying the same equipment, right? So we were able to work together. The schools have recently gotten a very good pricing point negotiating with one of the primary vendors for the wireless access points. And now we're able also to have that conversation with the same, they call them OEM, so original equipment manufacturer, about getting that additional discount just like them.

So I think a lot of the vendors have seen us coming in as a joint team. You know, we might be two different IT organizations, but we're one county. And so I think seeing that for the first time with a lot of our vendors was something significant. Granted, there are those places where, you know, they're not going to align because there's the educational, you know, benefits.

But we really did see a lot of economies of scale there. I think also one of the things that I want to add when we're talking about the other potentials was around SaaS products. So, we looked at the types of tools that we were using for monitoring, for digital certificates, and we found some opportunities there as well.

Granted, we might be on different renewal cycles for certain licensing, but we've been able to find some opportunities where we might be able to align in the future. Also, looking back to cloud data platforms, you know, we're very focused on data and our data analytics efforts.

We're focused on leveraging certain platforms for that. we talked with the schools, we looked at their strategy, what they're doing, and so we're also onboarding. This was a cost we were going to be spending anyway, and now we're spending it in the same trajectory in which the schools are going. This allows us also to have our staff, you know, learn from each other, right? So, like, we're learning the same, we're able to work closer together and really innovate together. So, I think those were some of the other really good opportunities that we found here once we started, you know, digging into the data. Additionally,

We really focused on that operational efficiency, which we are mindfully doing on a regular basis. So we have multiple technology procurements underway. So we have several large RFPs, RFPs for staff augmentation services, where we've had representatives from both the schools and the county as part of that selection advisory committee.

We're also sharing our cloud strategies, trying to find opportunities as well as we move forward with our different clouds and the different cloud platforms that we work with, aside from our own, you know, private cloud that we both maintain. And then we're also looking at joint application approaches.

You'll hear about it a little bit later when we talk more from the impact side. But as we look at that unified customer experience, that is something that we, it doesn't matter if you're a parent at a school or someone coming to Fairfax County to register or to do an athletic field schedule, you want to be able to have that seamless customer experience.

So we're looking for those other opportunities. Unfortunately, those are more in the longer term. However, the procurements are something that we're acting on right now. So next slide, again, just giving you some actual examples with a little bit of numbers. You know, we've seen growth from what the vendors have been willing to provide to us from 5% to 12% discounts increasing there.

We've also been able to say, okay, if we're strategically purchasing this hardware, X hardware together, you know, how can we receive those economies of scale? knowing that it's not a small one-time purchase, it's multiple purchases, and it's multiple, you know, products that we're buying together.

I think also we've seen vendors being more willing to work with us and to provide larger discounts for some of the, you know, emerging technologies that are already in our roadmaps. And we definitely have had an increased negotiating power when it comes to economies of scale.

And I do want to underscore, like, they're small wins, but they're important because each little small win adds up. And, you know, we're in this process of really dealing with some soaring technology costs. As mentioned, you know, probably before in the budget presentation, IT costs are growing.

And so by doing this, by being committed to being intentional about our collaboration, talking on a regular basis we're going to be able to help temper some of those rising costs and so finally kind of moving into what does our future look like so whereas I understand the Joint Committee was one point in time and we were you know aiming to you know have a culmination and a culmination report we're going to continue this collaboration right so the relationships are there relationships that we didn't know you know really existed much before we're We're going to continue to meet in April.

We really do have significant long-term planning discussions that we need to have. As Gouda mentioned, the aging facilities in which we have our data centers, that's hardware, that's location. There's a lot that we need to talk through.

We also, you know, we do have a private cloud, right, and that's reliant on that fiber. The fiber and the INET funding is based off of cable and cable bills. So as we know, more streaming services, that kind of thing. So all of these longer-term initiatives, we're going to really have to start coming together, understanding how we can work together to avoid some of those rising potential costs.

And as mentioned, again, we're working through those joint RFPs and then our cable infrastructure. We're also approaching that one as well as a joint team. And I want to underscore the joint RFPs. Yes, there's still a lot of work, but that's time that we're getting back on our calendars.

right? That's not two procurement offices going off and doing the same process and the same RFP. So we're saving time and effort and the expenditure from that standpoint. So we're not doubling efforts and reducing them. And oftentimes, I think we end up using the same vendors anyway. So this is really helping us save in the long run. And so with that, I know I ran through it rather quickly. I know there was a packed agenda. So that is pretty much all we have, and we're available for questions.

Okay. Thank you very much. Before I go on, I want to do one introduction. I forgot to do one of the things when I took over the IT committee was to fill the FCPS seat. So we did that in July. Guy Swope, you want a two-second introduction?

Yeah, my name is Guy Swope Been in the county for about 30 years been with a company called rtx Raytheon for about 30 years I support the CTO there directly and now supporting the ITPAC Helping represent FCPS on that particular committee. Thank you for that. And with that I will Jeremy have any comments and questions I'll save mine to the end. Yeah, I got just a couple questions and and my only comment is is you know again thank you for the presentation and the work i think the only other comment i'll make is is one that you referenced which is what i was i personally was largely hoping to get out of this

besides efficiencies and savings was a built relationship uh between the county and schools because honestly that has been too uh segmented in the past there have been walls up um you know having lived through the the covid pandemic we saw a lot of that really clearly um you know where where there were just walls between county and schools that were unnecessarily built.

And taking those down requires relationship building. And so I'm very hopeful that this continues. The committee will finish its work and be long gone, but the cooperative spirit between schools and county continues. And that's what our constituents expect and just assume that we're doing as a best practice.

And so that's my only comment of appreciation for that. I did have a couple of questions, But whenever I see somebody go to green, that means they want to say something. So let me let Alicia, if you wanted to say something on that point. I did want to highlight that.

One of the things we've really enjoyed is working with God and his team and Maura and Matt. We really just talked about the fact that that has been essential to our success going forward. It's built a foundation for us for continued cooperation, for enterprise-level discussions. And I really have appreciated that. And I think it's essential right now for all of us to sit down and think through things because we are facing insurmountable challenges both from the rising cost of things, but also just the complexity of all the things that we're trying to juggle.

So working together and utilizing our core expertise will make us that much better. So if nothing else comes out of the joint committee, which other things will, but the main thing that's coming out of it is that collaboration and relationship building. And unfortunately, Godam can't get away from us. So that's the good news, and I don't think he wants to at this point, but we're really excited about that.

And we appreciate it also -- I didn't say that at the beginning -- the board members from both the county board and the school board that work together because you provided support for us as well. So Supervisor Alcorn and Sork, and then Supervisor Sizemore Heiser, who started as a school board member but moved over, and then Sandy Anderson and Seema Dixit from the Fairfax County Public School Board because all of those things have really helped us. Your collaboration together as well as our collaboration is just setting us up for continued success. So thank you, Chairman, for putting this board matter forward.

Sure. Thank you. And the one question that I do have, and then I have a request maybe is the best way to put it. The question in terms of the vendors, a lot of this is written in a way that makes it sound like we're getting enhanced opportunities within the existing vending pool that we already use. And I know the OEM thing was brought up before, but I guess without naming names, what I'm interested in is, are we hearing from vendors outside of our normal pool? Are we open to talking to new people about new technologies, about ways to cost-save.

This is not pointed at any particular entity, individual, or agency, but I have heard overwhelmingly from the private sector that the barrier of entry for new technologies is pretty high in the county and that there seems to be, at least through the procurement process, loyalty to what I would call legacy procurements.

And, you know, again, I don't want to do procurement. I don't even want to know the names. I want to get a sense that the county's doors are wide open and that this new working relationship, stronger working relationship with schools is opening the door to potentially new and more interesting and maybe cost-saving vendors.

And if nothing else, what they do, of course, is drive down the cost with some of the legacy vendors that we do have. And so can you give us a sense of how this effort might enhance that? Yeah. To speak to that, we did, because our scope was narrow on current spend and what we know, which is in our, like, current roadmap of this year in FY27, we were focusing a lot on the current vendors that we work with. But in the discussions, there are different platforms and different, you know, technology services that both the schools use and that we use where we are looking to align and talk about new ways and new pathways. So I think

we are open. We're definitely interested in hearing from a lot of the vendors because, again, to your point, we had a lot of good competition when we're open to having that discussion. That does help. So we really, I think we're both open to it. I think we're trying to also make sure that we have those economies of scale when we're going into those conversations. As Maura had originally mentioned, the car ownership overlay, right? So some of the vendors or the resellers we were speaking to, they recognize that they can bring the same OEMs to us, but now they are trying to compete with each other. I think

we started signaling that we are one entity, which also then meant the vendors trying to compete with each other. We had on some of our calls, one of the vendors saying, hey, if you want to change the book of business to shift everything from the other reseller to us, we'll likely be able to get you larger discounts. So that is the beginning of the conversations. Obviously, you want to navigate this with procurement hand in glove, but that is happening already. Yeah, I think that's really important because it's one thing to negotiate a better deal with an existing vendor. It's another thing to use your buying power to get more people interested and drive down costs even more and be open to, you know, thinking about things outside the box. And so I think the message we need to

have out there is our doors are open and where there's an opportunity to compete, something we're going to compete it because we have new buying power now that we're going to use. We've had it before but we have it even in greater numbers now. And then my request, I guess, would be when you're looking at these opportunities to never lose sight of, in some cases, maybe we describe it as the end user, but I would say our customer because our kids are frustrated, our parents are frustrated about all the different systems and all the different logins and why our systems don't talk to each other on the school side. Our residents are frustrated that, you know, they can't use the

same platform to do multiple things in the county. I'm hoping that we're giving thought at the end of this to not only simplicity inside our government and school operations, but massive simplicity on the outside so that our users get a quality experience here. I mean, as a parent of two kids in FCPS, I still don't understand why they can't get a student ID that has a library card on it, has a Fairfax Connector user card already built into it because they're eligible in middle and high school and why they have to go three different places, or why when we looked at

trying to introduce fees for the SAC program, that one of the answers we got was that would be too hard to be able to implement because our NCS system would have to start talking to our SAC system, and at the end of the day, a parent just wants to go one place and transact all of that business, and so I hope that the efficiencies are internal, but they're also external so that our end users, customers, in our cases, our residents can get a benefit out of this as well. And that's my main request when we're looking at these things, to never lose sight of

that piece. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for both those questions. The legacy system thing, something that we're clearly heard and clearly working to overcome. And the focus on customer, we get a little bit of an update on the customer portal a little bit later. With that, let me just go down the line with super well we'll start with the two co-chairs supervisor Alcor thank you very much I do want to thank staff and and really this I think was a super helpful effort on a number of different levels and I know the the

purpose was narrow and focused and I'm glad that was retained but I think we're seeing now there are some longer-term things and benefits to both systems that that are going to, I think, reap benefits very much. And I appreciate very much the chairman's comments just now.

Hopefully, we can move more towards the back-end integration. And I realize there are data and privacy issues there that will have to be worked through over time. But thinking about more of a customer focus in terms of our residents, I couldn't agree more, you know, moving more towards that.

The other piece in terms of talking about purchasing power, I think it's important to note that we actually have an advantage in the public sector that the private sector does not have. Frankly, the county and the school system can team up and increase purchasing power. We don't have to worry about antitrust.

So frankly, I mean, this is something for the public benefit. So it is something I would encourage, you know, us to continue to do. And thinking about this over the longer term, I think they're probably – I'm not saying we're not going to keep this committee going, but ITPAC, I think, has a real opportunity to continue this momentum and to continue to provide input and encouragement for more integration and more efficiency.

So hopefully that also could be in the cards. So thank you very much. Yeah, and I agree with you on the ITPAC comment. And I think we're going to see a little bit of that a little bit later today. Supervisor Stork, did you have anything? Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
And I just want my colleagues to really understand or at least appreciate what we appreciated, which was this incredibly well-run committee support.

And the Deputy County Executive is here, Connor, just well done. I know Ms. Powers and you guys, it really was just incredibly well done, worked together. We were well, I think well briefed, but more importantly, we had the opportunity to ask the questions.

And I think automatically the way that it boiled down, I was kind of looking in page seven, I think this is clearly where we saw, I know you all brought this to us, but we saw automatically the core elements of that, which is the technical short-term side, which I think we're seeing a lot of that here, but also see the strategic side, which we know is maybe a real big bucks opportunity, but maybe not even so much big bucks, but is big service improvement opportunities, which is, in the end, if we use IT right, I know you all know this better than any of us, it saves money that we don't even know that we've saved

money on because it's just stuff that changes over time because, frankly, our customers are doing frankly more of the work but feeling better about it because they're able to do it more easily and effectively and then even calling a line or whatever and getting that support.

So I think those are key parts that I wanted especially to let obviously tell all of you but also make sure our colleagues understand that and Mr. Chairman of the board I think the sense that you had in putting this together I think was right on and I think we're seeing some of those benefits. So, I think I want to particularly congratulate you, Jeff, for that foresight, and I think we're seeing that. I know that we have some other opportunities still, and I guess I wanted to understand maybe a little bit better, how do you see the discounts coming

forward? I mean, we have small discounts, you know, 5 or 10 percent. Are there bigger opportunities, savings to get, obviously, a better outcome for our residents, whether it's services, but even more importantly, the cost of operations for us? I would say, just listen to the comments today, right? It's going to be twofold. There will be the hard cost savings, which will be the discounts when we have shared overlays of technology or hardware or services. But the value generation is probably going to be the long-term question here. How do we generate value for our citizens,

for parents, for community, by sharing these resources. I think that value has not a cost basis to it, but has an output basis which enhances the services because that's what we all do. In public service, we are essentially creating the technologies to serve the needs of the purpose of the organization.

In our cases, delivering education, preparing students for the future in that same realm, making it easy so our diverse communities can engage with the technologies that we provide. We have multiple pathways through that. And we start thinking through in terms of architectural alignment, which is where the deeper conversations are, right?

Because we have our own plumbing. FCG has their own plumbing. When you bring these two things together, you have to spend some time connecting the dots. I think that value in the next few months or a year is going to help us start looking at what does the future plumbing look like for the entire county, which ensures that information can flow through but also be gated where it needs to be for privacy and security purposes.

should we think about capturing that at least so, again, so our customers, really the folks of Fairfax County, understand that. I mean, it's kind of like going back to Chairman McKay's comments earlier about they see 66 new positions.

You know, how can we help them understand how we are doing this and what it can mean for them? They may see it in their use, but so I want to capture some of that, if you will, savings as well as I want to use that to leverage more, frankly, costs, discounts in lots of different ways.

Is there a particular way that we can quantify that, if you will, a performance indicator that we can look at that we can say here's what this was and here's – we thought we'd get X percent and we can get X plus Y percent? I mean, I think we can start looking at that and really come to it from like a KPI perspective because I think that is really what you're asking for.

So there is some sort of metric or a way in which the public can understand how we're realizing the benefits of this effort and the benefits of our continued collaboration. You know, I will make sure to add some comments around that into our NIP about how we plan on moving forward, especially how we plan on moving forward within the next year and then how we'll move forward kind of beyond that.

Because I do think we're going to have to come back to you guys and kind of give you an update on some of those things. I think you'll see as well the discussions that are coming up in some of that long-term planning, right? So the data center conversation, aligning our architectures, the plumbing that Gautam was speaking to, those are going to be potentially, you know, large, I think, investments at one time.

And so, therefore, we'll be able to be, like, preemptive with some of the, you know, what does that mean to the community? How does working together help us improve that experience for them? And Gautam alluded to it as well.

I do think that customer experience is a big piece. And you saw in one of the examples, athletic field scheduling. People don't care if it's a school field or a county field. And so just that one simple thing would be something we could show as it relates to a way to be more efficient and effective and make their life a little bit easier as they integrate with or interact with Fairfax County.
